content: Torticollis, also known as wry neck, is a condition characterized by the tilting of the head to one side, with the chin elevated and turned toward the opposite side. In children, torticollis can be either congenital or acquired. Congenital Muscular Torticollis The exact cause of congenital muscular torticollis is not well understood. It is thought to result from birth trauma or an abnormal position in the uterus, which can damage the sternocleidomastoid muscle in the neck. This damage leads to shortening or excessive contraction of the muscle, often accompanied by a limited range of motion in both rotation and lateral bending. The head typically tilts toward the affected muscle and rotates toward the opposite side. In some cases, a mass, known as a sternomastoid tumor, may be observed in the affected muscle. This mass usually appears between two to four weeks of age and gradually disappears, although the muscle may sometimes become fibrotic. The condition often resolves within the first five to eight months of life. Initial treatment involves physical therapy, including stretching exercises to address muscle tightness, strengthening exercises to restore muscular balance, and techniques to encourage symmetry. A TOT (Tubular Orthosis for Torticollis) collar may sometimes be used. Approximately 5–10% of cases require surgical intervention, such as a surgical release of the muscle, if physical therapy fails. Infants with torticollis are at an increased risk of developing plagiocephaly (flattening of the skull). Strategies to prevent this include altering the infant's head position during sleep, using a supportive pillow, and providing ample supervised tummy time while awake. Other less common causes of torticollis, such as tumors, infections, ophthalmologic issues, or other abnormalities, should be ruled out. For example, ocular torticollis caused by cranial nerve IV palsy should not be treated with physical therapy, as the torticollis in this case is a neurologic adaptation to maintain binocular vision. Treatment should instead focus on correcting the imbalance in the extraocular muscles. If torticollis is not corrected, facial asymmetry may develop. It is important to address the head position before adulthood, as improvements are more likely before the age of 18. Younger children tend to show the best outcomes. While congenital torticollis typically presents in infancy, it can be diagnosed later in life, even in adults who were not identified as infants or children. The term torticollis translates to wry neck. Acquired torticollis differs from congenital torticollis and can affect individuals of all ages. Acquired Torticollis Acquired torticollis arises due to an underlying issue and typically occurs in previously healthy children. Common causes include: Trauma to the neck, which can result in atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation. This condition involves the sliding of the two vertebrae closest to the skull, leading to ligament tears. Treatment involves traction to reduce the subluxation, followed by bracing or casting until the ligaments heal. Tumors of the skull base, such as posterior fossa tumors, which can compress the nerves supplying the neck muscles and cause torticollis. These cases require surgical treatment. Infections in the posterior pharynx, which can irritate the nerves supplying the neck muscles and lead to torticollis. Mild infections may be treated with antibiotics, but severe or intractable cases may require surgical debridement. Ear infections or surgical removal of the adenoids, which can lead to Grisel’s syndrome. This condition involves subluxation of the upper cervical joints, particularly the atlantoaxial joint, due to inflammatory laxity of the ligaments caused by infection. Treatment may involve manipulation of the neck or surgical resection. Certain medications, such as antipsychotics, can induce torticollis. Other rare causes of torticollis also exist. Evaluation The evaluation of a child with torticollis begins with a detailed history, including circumstances surrounding birth and any history of trauma or associated symptoms. Physical examination typically reveals decreased rotation and bending to the side opposite the affected muscle. Some studies suggest that congenital cases more frequently involve the right side, though this is not universally agreed upon. A thorough neurologic examination is essential, and associated conditions such as developmental dysplasia of the hip and clubfoot should be assessed. Radiographs of the cervical spine should be obtained to rule out obvious bony abnormalities, and MRI may be considered if structural problems or other conditions are suspected. An ophthalmologic evaluation should also be considered to rule out vision-related causes of torticollis, such as cranial nerve IV palsy or nystagmus-associated null position. Most cases in infants respond well to physical therapy. Other causes should be treated as appropriate based on the underlying condition. Torticollis in Adults Wry neck can also occur in adults due to various reasons, such as neck injuries or sleeping in an awkward position. Upon waking, individuals may find it extremely difficult or painful to move or lift their head. Torticollis in Animals Torticollis can also occur in animals, often as a result of inner ear infections or, less commonly, injuries. It is most commonly observed in domestic rodents and rabbits but can also occur in dogs and other animals.
